summary:
Same-sex activity is criminalised across Tanzania. Under the Penal Code as revised by the Sexual Offences (Special Provisions) Act 1998, section 138A treats 'gross indecency' between men as an offence carrying one to five years' imprisonment or a fine of TSh 100,000 to 300,000, and the maximum penalty available for same-sex conduct between men is life imprisonment. Heterosexual oral and anal sex are also offences under the same framework.

The semi-autonomous island jurisdiction of Zanzibar operates its own criminal statute, the Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004, enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives, so a visitor may fall under two overlapping criminal-law regimes depending on location. Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934, as amended in 2004, outlaws sex between women with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment or a TSh 500,000 fine, and defines 'gross indecency' broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania. A partner cannot be sponsored for entry, inherited from, or recognised as next of kin on the basis of a relationship status, and adoption is restricted to a married couple, so a same-sex couple cannot adopt jointly.

Enforcement has taken the form of organised persecution. In 2018 a 'witch hunt' against gay people was declared in Dar es Salaam, where gay men were forced to undergo anal examinations and were tortured; the Dar es Salaam Regional Commissioner, Paul Makonda, announced a 17-strong committee of police, lawyers and doctors tasked with identifying and punishing homosexuals and scouring the internet for videos of supposedly LGBTQ people. In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS groups on the basis of 'promoting homosexuality', directly disrupting services.

Amnesty International's January 2024 report, 'We Are Facing Extinction', documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people at national level, within a documented climate of discrimination that limits how far rights can be enjoyed in practice. Proposed legislation on same-sex relations was deferred after protests.

In June 2024 the UN Human Rights Office condemned as 'horrendous' the attack on Mauzinde, a Tanzanian transgender activist from Rahaleo: she was abducted by 12 men and found beaten in a forest with her ears cut. The UN called for bold action to combat discrimination against LGBTIQ+ people and flagged possible violations of ICCPR article 20 and the equality guarantees of Tanzania's Constitution under article 13.

OONI measurement data published in a 2024 report, 'Tanzania: Surge in online LGBTIQ censorship', documents state-directed blocking of LGBTIQ websites, social networks and rights sites, constraining access to information of direct use to LGBT visitors and residents.

A 2013 Human Rights Watch and Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition report documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old gay man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. A 2020 interview with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists records substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence and the denial of basic rights.

Health services carry formal non-discrimination duties: the 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to services regardless of 'age, parity, marital status, creed, race, color, or sexual preference'; the Nursing and Midwifery (Practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care based on sexual orientation; and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory care. Tanzania's HIV/AIDS rate is high, with roughly one million people infected.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department's 2013 Human Rights Report identified the three most widespread human rights problems in Tanzania as security-force use of excessive force, gender-based violence including FGM/C, and lack of access to justice, and separately listed discrimination based on sexual orientation and societal violence against persons with albinism. That report also details police custody abuse and describes the overall human rights record as poor, a backdrop that shapes how a LGBT complaint is likely to be handled.

Government respect for freedom of speech and freedom of assembly is described as declining, and UN human rights defenders in Tanzania may not make public statements supporting tolerance for fear of reprisals. Broadcast content regulations issued in 2018 bar inciting hatred on grounds of sexual preference; online content regulations of the same year banned such hate speech but were completely repealed by the 2020 online content regulations. The Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals still bars hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation.

Public advocacy carries measurable cost. Activists including Maria Sarungi Tsehai, Fatma Karume, Mwanahamisi Singano, Carol Ndosi, Zara Kay, Khalifa Said and Goodluck Haule have openly backed LGBTQ rights against officials such as Magufuli, Paul Makonda, Ally Hapi and Hamisi Kigwangalla, who pushed persecution. When the 2018 Dar es Salaam crackdown was announced the Foreign Ministry said it lacked government support, and Denmark withheld 65 million kr (about US$9.8 million) in aid.

There are no gay bars in Tanzania, although some venues exist where gay men meet, and lesbians are less visible than gay men. Social venues therefore offer little of the informal verification available elsewhere, and visibility patterns differ by gender.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the mainland Penal Code and, on the islands, the Zanzibar Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004, so prosecution risk attaches to ordinary private conduct rather than only to visible advocacy. The same absence of legal recognition shapes inheritance, medical decision-making and next-of-kin status for resident couples, and joint adoption is unavailable to unmarried and same-sex couples alike.

Documented abuse in custody is a resident-facing concern rather than a visitor-only one: the 2013 Human Rights Watch and Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition report recorded rape, beating and electric-shock style torture by police, and the anal-examination practices of 2018 were imposed on gay men in Dar es Salaam.

Service provision for people living with HIV has been interrupted by enforcement action, notably the October 2017 deportation of HIV/AIDS organisation staff on 'promoting homosexuality' grounds, even as national guidelines from 2013, 2010 and 2017 impose non-discrimination duties on family-planning and nursing services.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Tanzania was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the criminalisation findings above are therefore sourced to other inventories, and the profile's own framing of penalties remains unverified for this pass.

Whether the mainland maximum of life imprisonment has been applied in a reported conviction in recent years is not established in the available sources; the inventory supplies the statutory maximum and the section 138A range but no case-level sentencing data.

The inventory states no youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family-planning counselling language, and does not resolve how Zanzibar's statute is enforced against visitors in practice or whether mainland authorities recognise island convictions.
